item.title: Software Engineering Methods (SENG301)
item.description: This is the second course on software engineering after students learned about more classical development processes, software modelling and object orientation. This lecture-based course is composed by two distinct parts. I share the duty with another colleague and I mainly focus on the software development aspects (e.g., processes, team work, quality assessment). The first half is about teaching the Agile Software Development philosophy, un-teaching it and re-teaching it again. My colleague focuses on (object oriented) implementation aspects such as design patterns and advanced OO principles (e.g., Liskov, contracts).

item.title: Artificial Intelligence for Software Engineering (AI4SENG)
item.description: This project investigates the usage of AI/ML/NLP tools to support software development.

item.title: ScrumBoard
item.description: A web-based Scrum project management tool built for software engineering education, with typical project management features (backlog, sprint planning, task boards, burndown charts), LDAP-based or on-premise identity management, GitLab integration (for task work-logs), and form management for student reflections.

item.title: Software Engineering Team Project (SENG302)
item.description: This course is very different from a typical lecture-based teaching experience. Few lecture sessions are organised and the students are put in teams where they are immersed in a industry-like project. Every 3 to 4 weeks, teams deliver a shippable product that they demonstrate and review with the product owner and other teams. Technical workshops are organised to teach about continuous integration (and a little bit of DevOps), code review and unit and automated acceptance testing (including Test-Driven Design).

item.title: Django Vulnerability Injector
item.description: Automatically injects OWASP Top 10:2021 vulnerabilities into a Django app, turning it into a ready-made environment for hands-on cybersecurity training. Under development to extend to Top 10:2025.

item.title: Model-Driven for Agile Software Development (MDE4ASD)
item.description: This project is about bringing more modelling practices into agile software development. We look into generating models from textual documents (e.g., user stories) for further analysis, or extracting information from discussions on messaging apps. Here’s a list of the publications in that area. You can find some resources on our gitlab repository.

item.title: WASAF
item.description: Crawls a web application and fuzzes the endpoints and forms it discovers. A three-step pipeline: a Playwright-based crawler explores pages and DOM states (with support for authenticated sessions), a fuzzer runs SecLists payloads against the discovered endpoints and form fields, and a triage step sorts the findings into vulnerability classes. Evaluated against OWASP Juice Shop, where it reliably detects (No)SQL injections.

item.title: Meta Studies Web App
item.description: Helps researchers manage and screen papers for systematic reviews and meta-analyses, with collaborative yes/no/maybe decisions, role-based access, sampling, exporting to CSV, and duplicate detection.

item.title: Software Security (SENG406)
item.description: Building secure software is an intricate task that involves careful design of both preemptive and corrective measures. This course covers the secure development lifecycle where students learn about techniques to model security threats, follow secure coding standards and perform security-focused testing to prevent software to expose vulnerabilities. Students learn how to combine tools of various natures to identify threats as part of a continuous integration pipeline. The course also addresses data privacy and governance issues, including (indigenous) data sovereignty principles.

item.title: Software Testing
item.description: A recent interest sparkled in software testing and more particularly, in the broader scope of DevOps-friendly software development processes. The goal is to understand how to better support software testers through better practices, methods and more automation. See also our gitlab repository.

item.title: Simple PlantUML Web App
item.description: A lightweight, self-hosted split-pane editor for PlantUML diagrams with live preview - all rendering happens locally for privacy. Use a sandbox to run PlantUML on the server.

item.title: Past courses
item.description:
Software Engineering Research Project (SENG402)

This course is the capstone project for software engineering students. Students must work individually on either a staff or sponsored project that includes some aspects of research (e.g., user study, application of latest research results in an industrial context, proof-of-concepts). Students are supervised by an academic staff member and, when relevant, by an industry sponsor. Students deliver a project plan, an interim and a final report on top of a public presentation and a formal demonstration.

item.title: Markdown Web Viewer
item.description: A Django app for writing, versioning, and publicly sharing markdown documents, with live collaborative editing.

item.title: Scrumboard - A Jira-ersatz to teach agile software development
item.description: Over the past few years, we’ve been developing a web-based tool to support students tracking their progress in an agile software development course. In this blog, I’ll explain why we moved away from professional / industry-grade tools and decided to (not) reinvent the wheel.

item.title: Good coding practices need an advocate inside the team (or it won't work)
item.description: A few years ago, we looked into how teams deal with the technical debt in a software engineering project course (DOI to paper). One of the main takeaway from the focus group that followed an extensive data analysis (of the evolution of the quality of the code of 8 teams) and a survey (with 25 responses, being 40-ish % of the class) is that the adoption of clean code practices seem to be strongly influenced by a charismatic and engaged “team leader”. From a literature review (to appear soon at EASE, preprint here), we observed that the same pattern, i.e. the need for strong advocates in teams, exist for automated software testing in industry context. From these two studies, I believe that “old” XP advocates actually got it right and we have failed miserably to listen to them. Therefore, we felt into the same trap as before, i.e. process rigidity and putting the process before the people (and when I say “we”, I think education and industry).

item.title: Teaching about Scrum with paper
item.description: I’ll talk about how we teach about Scrum events and principles in a gamified context. First of all, the whole credit goes to Sonja Hof et al.. You may check their paper (just click on Sonja’s name, it’s a hyperref) that we modified a little and tried to adapt to fix the issues they witnessed in their experiment. One day, I actually should try to contact that team to see if they still do this tutorial and if they changed anything.

item.description: This year I tried something “revolutionary”: asking my third year students to read some material before coming to class. Well, I must admit, this has had mixed success and here is why.
